claims.text: Rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi has a dual-phase microstructure containing an fcc FeCoNi matrix and a hexagonal C14 Laves phase.
The C14 Laves phase is enriched in Ti and Fe-Co-Ni.
The fcc phase exhibits ferromagnetic ordering transitions near 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K.
Coexistence with the C14 phase induces antiferromagnetic coupling between Fe, Co, and Ni sublattices and the Ti-rich Laves phase.
Antiferromagnetic exchange coupling occurs at fcc/C14 boundaries and within Ti-rich sublattices of the C14 phase.
The antiferromagnetic coupling reduces net spin alignment and thereby suppresses the saturation magnetization attributed to the fcc phase.
Fcc/C14 interfaces act as strong domain-wall pinning sites.
The distinct crystal and electronic structure of the C14 phase increases magnetic anisotropy in the dual-phase alloy.
The C14 phase creates local strain fields that impede domain-wall motion.
Exchange-bias effects at fcc/C14 interfaces contribute to enhanced coercivity.
The orbital-moment limitation of the fcc phase is partially compensated or overcome by C14-induced anisotropy and the C14 phase's electronic structure.
The C14 phase acts as a magnetic hardening agent.
The dual-phase alloy can reach a coercivity of approximately 667 Oe at 400 K.
The dual-phase alloy has lower saturation magnetization than a single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni counterpart.
Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys have coercivity capped at 100 Oe.
The 100 Oe coercivity limit in single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni alloys is caused by insufficient orbital moments.
The proposed hardening mechanism is effective only when the C14 phase forms a continuous or semi-continuous network at fcc interfaces.
Excessive C14 content can cause brittleness or loss of ferromagnetic connectivity.
A C14-dominant alloy should have significantly lower coercivity than the dual-phase alloy if interfacial pinning is the principal hardening mechanism.
